claim: The distribution of antibiotic use across the population is uneven, with some individuals having no antibiotic pharmacy claims and others having many.
source: First, we described the distribution of antibiotic use across the population and showed that it is uneven, as some individuals had no antibiotic pharmacy claims and others had many.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the original analysis (Olesen et al., 2018) as referenced in the manuscript.

claim: There is no evidence that repeat use of antibiotics is more strongly associated with resistance than first use at the population level.
source: In our analysis, we found no evidence that repeat use was more strongly associated with resistance.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' data analysis presented in their original study.

claim: Antibiotic stewardship should not necessarily focus their attention on a few, high-consuming antibiotic users.
source: If true, these results imply that antibiotic stewardship should not necessarily focus their attention on a few, high-consuming antibiotic users.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that repeat use is not more strongly associated with resistance than first use.

claim: Outpatient prescribers do not in general rationally account for resistance rates.
source: As outpatient prescribers do not in general rationally account for resistance rates (Simpson et al., 2007), we are not convinced that reverse causality dominates.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Simpson et al., 2007.

claim: The degree to which clinicians alter their antibiotic prescribing practice in response to local rates of antibiotic resistance is an empirical question.
source: However, the degree to which clinicians alter their antibiotic prescribing practice in response to local rates of antibiotic resistance is an empirical question, and our debate could be resolved by better direct quantification of reverse causality.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the scientific question and what would be needed to resolve it.

claim: High population-level resistance against an antibiotic would discourage rational prescribers from both first and repeat use of that antibiotic.
source: We expect that high population-level resistance against an antibiotic would discourage rational prescribers from both first and repeat use of that antibiotic.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how rational prescribers would behave in response to resistance rates.

claim: In cases of low population-level resistance, rational prescribers would be more discouraged against repeat use than first use, because resistance may arise because of antibiotic exposure in that patient.
source: In contrast, in cases of low population-level resistance, rational prescribers would be more discouraged against repeat use than first use, because resistance may arise because of antibiotic exposure in that patient.
evidence: This is an inference about prescriber behavior based on the biological mechanism of resistance development.

claim: Prior antibiotic use is a more important risk factor for patient-level resistance when population-level resistance is low compared to when population-level resistance is high.
source: In other words, prior antibiotic use is a more important risk factor for patient-level resistance when population-level resistance is low compared to when population-level resistance is high.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between individual and population-level resistance dynamics.

claim: Reverse causality, when population-level resistance affects individual-level prescribing, would have a greater influence on first use than repeat use.
source: We therefore expect that reverse causality, when population-level resistance affects individual-level prescribing, would have a greater influence on first use than repeat use.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preceding arguments about prescriber behavior.

claim: The associations between first use and resistance observed in the original analyses, which tended to be positive, are actually underestimates of the forward-causal effect of antibiotic use on resistance.
source: If this is true, then the associations between first use and resistance we observed in our original analyses, which tended to be positive, are actually underestimates of the forward-causal effect of antibiotic use on resistance, in fact strengthening the interpretation of our original result that first use has a more important forward-causal effect on resistance than repeat use.
evidence: This is a conditional inference based on the preceding argument about reverse causality affecting first use more than repeat use.

claim: The associations between repeat use of an antibiotic and resistance to that antibiotic tend to be negative.
source: In the original analyses (Olesen et al., 2018), we found that the associations between repeat use of an antibiotic and resistance to that antibiotic tend to be negative.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' original data analysis.

claim: Pouwels et al., 2019 found that associations between overall repeat antibiotic use and resistance to particular classes of antibiotics tend to be positive.
source: Re-analyzing our data, Pouwels et al., 2019 found that associations between overall repeat antibiotic use and resistance to particular classes of antibiotics tend to be positive.
evidence: This is a finding from Pouwels et al.'s reanalysis, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Focusing on overall antibiotic use limits the role of reverse causality.
source: Although we generally agree with their logic about how focusing on overall use limits the role of reverse causality, we expect that focusing on overall use limits the role of forward causality as well.
evidence: This is an inference about how different analytical approaches affect causal interpretation.

claim: Focusing on overall antibiotic use limits the role of forward causality.
source: Although we generally agree with their logic about how focusing on overall use limits the role of reverse causality, we expect that focusing on overall use limits the role of forward causality as well.
evidence: This is an inference about how different analytical approaches affect causal interpretation.

claim: It is not clear whether reverse causality is limited to a greater degree than forward causality when focusing on overall antibiotic use.
source: It is not clear to us that reverse causality is limited to a greater degree than is forward causality.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the relative effects of analytical approach on causal interpretation.

claim: In the absence of reverse causality, use of antibiotic A should be a better predictor for resistance to A than use of any antibiotic, even given co-selection and other mechanisms by which use of other antibiotics can select for resistance to antibiotic A.
source: In the absence of reverse causality, use of antibiotic A should be a better predictor for resistance to A than use of any antibiotic, even given co-selection and other mechanisms by which use of other antibiotics can select for resistance to antibiotic A.
evidence: This is an inference based on biological mechanisms of antibiotic resistance selection.

claim: Using overall first use as a predictor dilutes forward causality.
source: In other words, using overall first use as a predictor dilutes forward causality.
evidence: This is an inference about how the choice of predictor variable affects causal interpretation.

claim: A high resistance rate to a first-line therapy will mean that, on average, more unique antibiotics will be required to cure the infection.
source: Pouwels et al., 2019 mentioned that a high resistance rate to a first-line therapy will mean that, on average, more unique antibiotics will be required to cure the infection.
evidence: This is a logical inference about treatment patterns in the context of resistance, attributed to Pouwels et al., 2019.

claim: Overall repeat use captures drug-switching, emphasizing reverse causality: when resistance to an antibiotic is high for a given pathogen, more antibiotic prescriptions, especially for antibiotics of different classes, will be used to treat infections due to that pathogen.
source: Overall repeat use captures this drug-switching, emphasizing reverse causality: when resistance to an antibiotic is high for a given pathogen, more antibiotic prescriptions, especially for antibiotics of different classes, will be used to treat infections due to that pathogen.
evidence: This is an inference about how the analytical approach captures a particular causal pathway.

claim: It is unclear why overall repeat antibiotic use should have a stronger forward-causal, biologically selective effect on resistance to a particular class of antibiotics, compared to repeat use of antibiotics in that particular class.
source: As with first use, it is unclear to us why overall repeat antibiotic use should have a stronger forward-causal, biologically selective effect on resistance to a particular class of antibiotics, compared to repeat use of antibiotics in that particular class.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the biological mechanisms underlying the observed associations.

claim: There is a lack of strong evidence about the role of antibiotic resistance in prescribers' decisions to switch antibiotic treatments for a patient.
source: Again, however, the lack of strong evidence about the role of antibiotic resistance in prescribers' decisions to switch antibiotic treatments for a patient limits a productive debate.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: There are many confounders, data problems, and open methodological questions that may limit the applicability of the results for determining public health policy.
source: In contrast to the above, we heartily agree with the final point of Pouwels et al., 2019 that there are many confounders, data problems, and open methodological questions that may limit the applicability of our results for determining public health policy.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations, agreeing with points raised by Pouwels et al., 2019.

claim: Estimates of antibiotic resistance in the US rely on convenience samples of hospital antibiotic resistance reports.
source: We also applaud efforts to generate more reliable data sources so that estimates of antibiotic resistance in the US need not rely on, as we did, a convenience samples of hospital antibiotic resistance reports.
evidence: This is a description of the data sources used in the original study.

claim: Today's public health policy must proceed based on the best available evidence.
source: However, in the meantime, we hold that today's public health policy must proceed based on the best available evidence.
evidence: This is a normative statement about how public health policy should be conducted.

claim: Previous reports speculated that repeat use would have a greater effect on population-level antibiotic resistance than first use.
source: Previous reports speculated that repeat use would have a greater effect on population-level antibiotic resistance than first use, in other words, that 'intensive' use of antibiotics in a few people is more important for resistance than 'extensive' use across many people.
evidence: This references speculation from previous literature.

claim: Research into the epidemiology of antibiotic resistance will benefit from further study of individual prescriber behavior in response to patient-level risks and population-level prevalence of antibiotic resistance.
source: We take this as an overall sign that research into the epidemiology of antibiotic resistance will benefit from further study of individual prescriber behavior in response to patient-level risks and population-level prevalence of antibiotic resistance.
evidence: This is an inference about future research directions based on the current debate.

claim: The disagreements between the authors and Pouwels et al. depend on remarkably subtle arguments about specific aspects of prescriber behavior and its role in reverse causality.
source: Although we disagree on certain points, discussed below, we note that our disagreements depend on remarkably subtle arguments about specific aspects of prescriber behavior and its role in reverse causality.
evidence: This is a characterization of the nature of the scientific debate.

claim: The original analysis characterized the landscape of correlations between antibiotic use and resistance for antibiotics and many pathogens.
source: Second, we characterized the landscape of correlations between antibiotic use and resistance for antibiotics and many pathogens.
evidence: This describes a component of the original analysis.

claim: The original analysis investigated whether first or repeat antibiotic use is more strongly associated with resistance at the population level.
source: Third, we investigated whether first or repeat antibiotic use is more strongly associated with resistance at the population level.
evidence: This describes a component of the original analysis.

claim: A person's number of antibiotic pharmacy claims in a year can be partitioned into the sum of 'first use' and 'repeat use'.
source: To do so, we partitioned a person's number of antibiotic pharmacy claims in a year into the sum of 'first use' – zero if the person had no claims for that antibiotic, one if they had at least one claim – and 'repeat use', the number of claims beyond the first.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the original analysis.

claim: First use is defined as zero if the person had no claims for that antibiotic, one if they had at least one claim.
source: To do so, we partitioned a person's number of antibiotic pharmacy claims in a year into the sum of 'first use' – zero if the person had no claims for that antibiotic, one if they had at least one claim – and 'repeat use', the number of claims beyond the first.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the analysis.

claim: Repeat use is defined as the number of claims beyond the first.
source: To do so, we partitioned a person's number of antibiotic pharmacy claims in a year into the sum of 'first use' – zero if the person had no claims for that antibiotic, one if they had at least one claim – and 'repeat use', the number of claims beyond the first.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the analysis.

claim: Pouwels et al., 2019 argue that reverse causality dominates over forward causality in associations between antibiotic use and resistance.
source: First, they argue that reverse causality (rational prescriber response to local resistance rates) dominates over forward causality (the biological selection for resistance) in associations between antibiotic use and resistance, so that our analytical results about the relationships between first use, repeat use, and antibiotic resistance do not support our conclusions about how antibiotic stewardship should be performed.
evidence: This summarizes an argument made by Pouwels et al., 2019.

claim: Pouwels et al., 2019 argue that the relative roles of forward and reverse causality differ for first and repeat use in a way that undermines the original conclusions.
source: Second, they argue that the relative roles of forward and reverse causality differ for first and repeat use in a way that further undermines our original conclusions.
evidence: This summarizes an argument made by Pouwels et al., 2019.

claim: Pouwels et al., 2019 argue that analyzing use of all antibiotics, rather than use of particular classes of antibiotics, changes the relative role of forward and reverse causality.
source: Third, they argue that analyzing use of all antibiotics, rather than use of particular classes of antibiotics, changes the relative role of forward and reverse causality and find evidence that, if this assumption were correct, would even further undermine our conclusions.
evidence: This summarizes an argument made by Pouwels et al., 2019.

claim: Overall first use (the proportion of people who claimed any antibiotic) is an indicator of how many patients require an antibiotic prescription.
source: With respect to first use, Pouwels et al., 2019 asserted that overall first use – that is, the proportion of people who claimed any antibiotic – is an indicator of how many patients require an antibiotic prescription.
evidence: This summarizes an assertion made by Pouwels et al., 2019.

claim: Overall first use should be less affected by antibiotic resistance levels than first use rates for any particular class of antibiotics.
source: This measure should be less affected by antibiotic resistance levels than first use rates for any particular class of antibiotics.
evidence: This is part of the logic presented by Pouwels et al., 2019 as described by the authors.

claim: Models of overall first use rather than first use of particular antibiotic classes should be less susceptible to reverse causality.
source: Thus, models of overall first use rather than first use of particular antibiotic classes should be less susceptible to reverse causality.
evidence: This is an inference about analytical approaches attributed to Pouwels et al., 2019.

claim: The finding of Pouwels et al., 2019 that overall repeat use is better associated with resistance than overall first use does not contradict the original finding that first use of individual antibiotic classes is better associated with resistance to those antibiotics than repeat use of those antibiotics.
source: If this is true, the finding of Pouwels et al., 2019 – that overall repeat use is better associated with resistance than overall first use – does not contradict our original finding – that first use of individual antibiotic classes is better associated with resistance to those antibiotics than repeat use of those antibiotics.
evidence: This is a conditional inference about the compatibility of different findings.
